\[
q = \operatorname{smooth}(p),
\quad
d = p - q,
\quad
p' = q + k\, d,
\qquad k = 5
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(p\): The input
- \(q\): The base layer, an edge-preserving smoothing of p
- \(d\): The detail layer
- \(k\): The boost

q is an edge-preserving smoothing of the input p, the base layer. The difference d is the detail layer, and p' adds it back k times. He, Sun and Tang show this with a detail layer boosted 5 times. Their guided filter uses r = 16 and eps = 0.1^2. Their bilateral filter uses sigma_s = 16 and sigma_r = 0.1, on values from 0 to 1. They note that the bilateral filter can reverse gradients near edges, while the guided filter does not. The bilateral base here is the piecewise-linear bilateral filter of Durand and Dorsey, also used for tone mapping, so its cost does not grow with sigma_s.
